For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and the new floor laid afterwards had been bought on credit from Harlan Dace, the builder. The club had been in debt to him ever since. Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, had other worries: rot was in the scoreboard's posts, and he wanted the scoreboard moved to higher ground.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but he would pay sixty pounds for the damaged pavilion as it was, cancel the debt, and cart the whole building off to his yard in the lower village for a barn. He had run a lemonade stand at every home match for years and knew the club's accounts nearly as well as the secretary did. The captain, Neil Pryor, wanted the roof repaired where it stood, but he had no figure to set beside Dace's.

The vote was ten to three for the offer. That spring, the minutes show, the subscriptions had come to less than the interest. In July Dace's men took the pavilion apart in numbered sections and carted it away, and the teas moved to a trestle table under the scoreboard by the river. Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let the cricketers use the village school hall for changing.

The barn is still in Dace's old yard, its veranda boarded in, and on a clear evening the faded letters ASKERBY C.C. can be made out above the door. The minutes for July 1962 give it a single line: "Pavilion removed." Old members who remember it talk mostly about teas on that veranda, and about the light going off the river from its top step on summer evenings long ago.

passage:
Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters in four days, so that Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, could repair its gates on the schedule she had set. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. But the gravel bar across the cove's mouth then stood a meter higher, and behind it a pool stayed knee-deep all winter; Kettle counted some six hundred live mussels in it. Floods have since worn the bar down.

It was Teo who proposed the plan the team followed. If the bar had held a pool once, he argued, it could again, and in two days volunteers from Wendle raised a wall of sandbags along its crest, sixty meters long. Kettle had offered to carry mussels out to the channel in buckets, but the wall would rescue every mussel at once. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, took two hundred mussels into her tanks as a reserve.

When the reservoir fell, the wall held. Behind it the cove stayed a meter deep while the water outside slid away toward the channel. Marrow checked the cove; by December she had found fewer than fifty dead shells inside the wall, and a handful outside it, stranded where they had tried to follow the falling waterline.

The wall still stands, as it must, since Vane expects to lower the reservoir again within three years. But sandbags settle, split and slump, and every storm that comes down the valley now brings Hollin Cove one question: whether the wall will still be there when the water drops.
